cards.title: Write a one-paragraph messaging strategy before any copy
cards.summary: A short written messaging strategy gives every copy and design decision a rationale so you stop choosing words by what 'sounds good'.
cards.use_when: You are about to write or rewrite PDP copy, homepage copy or ad creative for a store and need a shared standard for what the copy should do, especially when several people or freelancers touch it.
steps: Before writing any copy, write down the guiding principles your copy must follow as a short document. Joanna Wiebe's example for Page99Test.com is a single paragraph: copy is 'short, friendly and to the point', assumes visitors want to read book excerpts not marketing copy, keeps words to a minimum, and wherever a screenshot, press logo, button, video demo or icon can be used it should replace copy without sacrificing clarity.

Pick the principles that matter for your store from the source's list of candidate principles: let copy guide design because good writing is good design; some visitors want to read a lot and some don't, and both are customers; support messages with social proof like testimonials or media reviews; support key concepts with video demonstrations; just because you say it doesn't make it true, so prove it; strive for clarity above cleverness; let the message match the medium at an exact point of need; all visitors can be persuaded to join or upgrade; engage visitors with content, experiences or mobile/app options.
Treat the document as a living document, not etched in stone: update it as you learn your customers' language and as you add or change products.
Share the strategy with designers, developers and freelancers so they understand your brand and messaging approach before they produce assets.
Draft your own version in one sitting without censoring yourself, then edit afterward rather than trying to reach a final version on the first, second or third try.
caveats: The source frames this for startups; a longer or more detailed strategy is not required for it to work.
The strategy governs copy, not formatting or layout — establish messages before formatting bullets, headlines and buttons.

cards.title: Lead With 'What's In It For Me?' Benefits
cards.summary: Consumers care about what the product does for them, not company facts, equipment or process.
cards.use_when: Reviewing product pages, about sections, ad copy or brochures that currently describe the company, factory or product specs.
steps: Audit each asset for self-serving content: company history, staff counts, square footage, equipment photos, 'unusual camera angles'. The source cites Daniel Starch's research showing readers ignore factory-focused ads.
For each feature listed, write the corresponding consumer benefit and lead with the benefit.
Put the single biggest benefit in the headline.
Batch benefits throughout ('Bombard Your Readers With Benefits') rather than relying on one strong claim.
Use the Flesch readability ease concept and clear layout so benefit statements land fast.
caveats: This is the book's core 'advertising should move people to act' doctrine—it is a direct-response stance, not a brand-awareness stance; brand campaigns may weight emotion and imagery differently.

cards.title: Choose whether to lead with a benefit or a feature per audience
cards.summary: There is no universal rule that copy must lead with the benefit — some shoppers distrust soft benefit language and go straight to comparison charts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what goes in the hero headline and first bullets of a PDP or landing page for a specific shopper type.
steps: Treat the top-priority message as your 'lead'. The source reports having seen a headline focused on a new product feature outperform a headline showing an expected benefit, so the decision is situational, driven by what your customer base needs at that moment.

Match the lead to shopper type. Some shoppers are suspicious of soft marketing messages — which many benefits unfortunately become. Others jump straight to comparison charts and catalogues to check the features. Others signed up because they heard about one cool feature. The source states none of these types would want you to lead with the benefit.

Whatever you lead with, support every feature with a benefit and every benefit with a feature or a related support point — the source's example of support is a snapshot of the interface design backing a benefit of enjoyable software.

Look at AnyNewBooks as a working pattern: the headline leads with the core benefit, the subhead supports it with the service feature of weekly notifications. The source derives at least three explicit benefits from that one feature: no cost so cash stays in your pocket; weekly cadence means no spam and no wasted seconds deleting emails; the emails come to you so you don't hunt for new books and risk missing something you would love.

Use a mix as Mint does on its How It Works page: the page headline speaks to features while addressing the overarching value proposition of power and simplicity, and the chunk headlines vary between benefits ('See all your accounts in one place', 'stay safe and secure') and features (autocategorization of transactions), each supported by a clear visual.
caveats: The source's cross-reference of feature-led versus benefit-led headline performance comes from the author's own observation, with no dataset, so it does not establish a general rule.

Do not summarize to fit a tight space: the source says a constrained copywriter should choose shorter, tighter words rather than dilute the message, because a summary is neither noticeable nor memorable and specifics stick.

cards.title: Abstract-to-Concrete Zoom-In Exercise
cards.summary: Rewrite vague benefits by drilling down a two-column abstract/concrete sheet until you hit a picturable object or scenario.
cards.use_when: Your product benefits read as adjectives ('effective', 'convenient', 'premium') and you need concrete claims for ads, PDP bullets or category positioning.
steps: Take a sheet of paper and draw a vertical line down the middle. Write 'abstract' at the top of the left column and 'concrete' at the bottom of the right.
Write your current vague phrase in the left column (e.g. 'regain fitness', 'pretty people in big cities').
Ask repeatedly, 'What do I actually mean here?' and rewrite the phrase lower and lower in the right column, converting intangible words into objects, people, places or actions a reader can picture.
Worked example from the source: 'regain fitness' becomes 'getting people up off the couch to run 5K' — the source notes this is effectively the Couch to 5K naming logic.
Second worked example: 'worn by pretty people in big cities and old people elsewhere' becomes 'worn by supermodels in London and dads in Ohio' — two picturable people in a funny juxtaposition.
Use the resulting concrete phrasing directly as product name, headline or PDP bullet candidates, then run the three-question copy test on each.

Sharpen concrete words further where possible: source critique of a Tesla line suggested preferring 'tougher than an F-150' over 'better truck than an F-150' for shorter, more picturable, more ownable phrasing.
caveats: Drilling down takes real work and multiple rewrites; the source notes 'you can't just like' produce facts — research is required.
Concrete wording can be less searchable or less category-obvious; you may need one concrete emotional line plus one plain functional line on the same PDP.
cards.source_name: Learn Copywriting in 76 Minutes – Harry Dry.docx

cards.title: The Psychology of Simplicity: Readable Copy Is Non-Negotiable
cards.summary: Advertising exists to get people to act, so it must be written to be understood - simple, direct, and readable.
cards.use_when: Final QA on ad copy, PDP text, email, and any customer-facing copy before it ships.
steps: Apply the foundational rule: write so people can understand. The source calls this the #1 key to all effective written communication, and warns that an incomprehensible effective message is equivalent to no ad at all.
Treat clarity as a prerequisite: you may be advertising, but until someone reads and understands, you're just talking to yourself - and you don't need to pay to do that.
Audit readability yourself before publishing. The source notes there's no magic to it: you write, run the test, examine the score, and edit until it hits the range you want.
Tighten sentences and reduce sentence length where the copy reads slowly. Long sentences can require fewer words overall but demand more mental processing, which loses readers.
caveats: The source argues this is the foundation for everything else in the book - skip it and other techniques won't rescue the ad.
Clarity work is not just correct grammar; wordy but grammatically perfect copy can still fail the test.

cards.title: Match the Brand's Actual Voice
cards.summary: Extract the brand's recurring language and promise from its own content instead of defaulting to generic hype phrasing.
cards.use_when: Writing emails or ads for a brand whose tone is clinical, expert, or understated rather than hype-driven.
steps: Read the brand's own content — social posts, website, podcast transcripts, support replies — and extract recurring phrases, themes, and the actual promise they make.

Diagnose mismatches: a money-saving finance voice talking about budgeting and making money go further is not going to say 'your dream life is 12 weeks away' — that is business-opportunity voice, not their voice.
Choose subject lines that paraphrase the brand's own language, e.g. 'this costs you thousands every year' fits a frugal-finance promise better than a vague dream-life slogan.
Note the source's finer point: he talks about dream finances first, and dream life as the downstream result — copy should respect that chain rather than jumping straight to the aspiration.
For a store, sample the brand's existing tone (packaging copy, support replies, product education posts) before writing promotional copy so the email doesn't sound like a different company.
caveats: This is the source's critique of one specific email, not a tested voice-conversion rule.
Hyperbolic voice is sometimes correct for courses and coaching offers — the guidance is fit, not absolute avoidance.

cards.title: Match Static Ad Format to Stage of Awareness
cards.summary: Most brands fail top-of-funnel by running product-aware or most-aware statics to cold, unaware audiences — instead lead cold traffic with education or problem agitation.
cards.use_when: Choosing which static ad concepts to produce for a cold prospecting campaign versus a retargeting campaign.
steps: Classify each concept by Eugene Schwartz awareness stage before producing it: most-aware/product-aware statics (plain product shots, 'guaranteed energy in 5 minutes') belong in retargeting, while unaware/problem-aware audiences need statics that lead with education or a named problem.
For cold audiences, open with a problem the viewer recognises rather than the product: the GLP-1 hair loss static leads with 'GLP1 hair loss hits hard' and only then introduces the supplement.
Use advertorial-style statics (native statics that look like content) to educate before the hard sell, since they let you agitate the problem without immediately demanding a purchase.

Check the mismatch symptom: a clean product shot with a benefit headline running against cold traffic is the format-audience mismatch the source names as the primary reason top-of-funnel statics fail.
Route each stage to the right destination — education/curiosity concepts need an educational landing page, while product-aware concepts can go to a standard PDP.
caveats: Awareness stages are used as a strategist's organising framework here; the source offers no measurement data linking stage to ROAS, so treat the alignment as a planning discipline rather than a proven lift.
cards.source_name: How To Make Better Meta Ads_ 8 Static Creatives Analysed.docx

cards.title: Match Image and Copy at the Same Awareness Stage
cards.summary: When the static image assumes one awareness stage and the copy speaks to another, the ad fails; the image and copy must sit at the same stage.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing static ad that is underperforming, or QA review before launch.
steps: Identify the awareness stage the static image assumes (e.g., a product shot means the viewer already knows the product).
Read the primary text and confirm it addresses the same audience; a product-aware image paired with solution-aware copy ('creatine helps you gain strength') will not convert.
When mismatch is found, correct either the image (to match the copy's stage) or the copy (to match the image's stage).
Use a story-based or agitate-based image with copy that speaks to the same problem and audience.
This diagnosis applies to video as well as static: the ad creative and the copy must align to avoid wasted spend.
caveats: The creatine example is the source's illustration; stage definitions come from Eugene Schwartz's awareness model referenced by the source.
cards.source_name: How to Make Static Image Ads That Scale in 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Verifiable Evidence to Convert Belief into Purchase
cards.summary: Evidence - facts, figures, testimonials, endorsements, research, charts - persuades more effectively than claims you made yourself.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for higher-priced or considered-purchase products where prospects need justification before buying.
steps: Use the source's operational definition: evidence is 'any factual statement, object, or opinion not created by the source that is used by that source as support' (Reinhard, 1988). Facts, figures, testimonials, endorsements, research, and charts qualify. Your own claims do not.

Layer evidence on top of emotional appeal. You must provoke emotion to get the prospect excited enough to spend, but especially for costlier products you must supply enough reasoning so they can justify the purchase and satisfy their sense of responsibility.

Present evidence clearly and simply. Peripheral thinkers - most readers - won't work through dense data; they'll scan, decide, and move on. Colorful charts and graphs, plus quotes from trusted professionals, let them absorb the proof fast.
Anticipate the source's key point: buyers want to believe your claims (because believing lets them enjoy the benefits), and strong evidence is what lets them give themselves permission.
caveats: The source argues evidence is most effective with important or expensive products where buyers think carefully. Lower-cost impulse goods may rely more on emotion.
Central-route thinkers will scrutinize and check your evidence - make sure it holds up.

cards.title: Mine real customer data for the objection-handling section
cards.summary: Populate the VSL objection section with verbatim customer reasons for almost-not-buying, drawn from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings.
cards.use_when: Writing the objection-handling portion of a VSL script for a product where buyers considered alternatives or hesitated before purchase.
steps: Pull from reviews, support tickets, post-purchase surveys, and call recordings the reasons people almost didn't buy or what they had already tried.

Map each reason to the script's objection-handling section: name the thing they tried and explain why it didn't work (e.g., gargling only rinses the surface and can't reach the deep biofilm where bacteria live).
Sequence this so the customer feels understood before you introduce the mechanism and product.
Use this miner approach rather than guessing at objections from internal assumptions.
caveats: Source frames this as its own recommended method; it does not provide a validated benchmark for how much objection handling lifts performance.
cards.source_name: The 7-Part VSL Framework for eCommerce (With Examples).docx

cards.title: Direct Mental Movies With Specific Visual Words
cards.summary: Replace vague benefit claims with specific visual language that makes prospects mentally simulate using the product.
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, ad body copy, landing page sections or video scripts where a generic benefit statement is falling flat.
steps: Start from a vague line ('Go somewhere and do something') and progressively add specificity: location, object, action, then sensory detail (the source's progression: go to the kitchen / open the oven / pull out the pizza / pull out the freshest, crispiest pizza you've ever eaten).
Use action verbs and concrete nouns so readers picture themselves performing steps with the product, not just reading a claim.
Add 'positive visual adjectives' (PVAs) sparingly at key moments to intensify the image.
Apply this to ecommerce PDPs: instead of 'high-quality nonstick pan', write copy that walks the buyer through the first meal they'll cook in it.

For video ads, script the sequence of images the viewer should see in their mind rather than listing features; the source's framing is that 'the first use of any product is inside the consumers' minds'.
caveats: Whitman's claim that imagery increases desire is a persuasion principle, not a measured conversion lift—test copy variants against your own baseline.
Overwriting dense imagery can hurt readability; the source also recommends clear readability formulas and simplicity.

cards.title: Feature-to-Benefit 'Big Deal' Translation
cards.summary: Convert every product spec into a WIIFM benefit by forcing each feature through the 'You benefit by…' test.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP bullets, bundle descriptions or ad copy from a spec sheet that currently lists only features.
steps: List each feature as a plain component (e.g., 'multiple ink tanks', '500-sheet tray', 'ultra-draft mode button').

For each, mentally shout 'BIG DEAL! What's in it for me?' then complete the sentence 'You benefit by…'. Example: multiple ink tanks → 'You benefit by saving money because you don't replace the whole cartridge when one color runs out.'
Keep the buyer's reaction as the copy — the source's printer example shows the prospect immediately self-identifies with the pain ('I spend a fortune for ink with my current printer').

Use the source's Rolls-Royce examples as the pattern: hand-selected leather → luxurious comfort in all climates; deep-pile wool carpeting → rich softness underfoot; 453-hp V-12 → power, control, supreme reliability; Spirit of Ecstasy hood ornament → feeling of power and 'arrived' status.
Run the same drill on every bundle or upsell item so cross-sell copy names the gain, not the components.
Strip anniversary notices, staff photos and company milestones unless they come with a price cut or buyer gain.
caveats: The feature/benefit split is the source's framing; a benefit that isn't credible becomes hype.
Do not convert a benefit into an unsupported numeric promise (e.g., 'save 50% on ink') unless your own product data supports it.

cards.title: Specific Headlines Over Clever Headlines for Paid Ads
cards.summary: Write ad headlines that state the offer and audience plainly rather than chasing cleverness, because clicks for the wrong reason convert to sales far less often.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing headlines for paid social, search, or display ads and deciding between a clever hook and a specific offer-based headline.
steps: Before finalizing, ask what the reader thinks you are selling after reading only the headline. If they cannot tell, rewrite.
Build the headline from the core elements: product/promise, key benefit, time-to-deliver or other qualifier, price or savings signal, and credibility (expert, years, results).

Check the headline against the audience it should attract. A clever hook like 'Sticky Web' may get clicks but from people who don't need the service; a specific headline attracts only qualified buyers.
Reserve cleverness for tests only, with a budget you're willing to risk; judge by qualified clicks and purchase conversion, not raw CTR.
Add psychological triggers via the source's 22 headline starters rather than puns, and put one clear benefit in the headline.
caveats: The source's position that 'clever' headlines lose 60% of scrollers is a heuristic, not verified by the source's own testing data.
Averages can mask brand-recall or entertainment-first campaigns where cleverness aids shareability, though the author disputes that framing.
